svg.title: How ScheduleEventDag::GetTopologicalOrdering picks the next event
svg.desc: Kahn's algorithm with a min-priority queue on job index, step by step on the example DAG, compared with the Boost DFS order Dag<T> would give.
svg.metadata: ["Start: count each event's incoming edges. a and e have none, so both go on the min-heap, keyed by job index: a (job 0), e (job 1).", "Pop a. a has the lowest job index (0) of the ready events. Popping it removes a -> b and a -> c; b now has no incoming edge and joins the heap.", "Pop b. b (job 0) beats e (job 1). Its edge b -> c goes, so c becomes ready.", "Pop c. c (job 0) beats e (job 1). Removing c -> d makes d ready.", "Pop d. d (job 0) is still ahead of e: job 0 finishes first wherever the edges allow.", "Pop e. Only e is ready. Popping it makes f ready.", "Pop f. f is last. Six events were popped, as many as the DAG has, so there is no cycle and the order is returned."]

text.font-family: 'IBM Plex Sans', 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif

g.text: Only the job index is compared, so among ready events of the same job the heap's internal order decides. That order is deterministic for a DAG built the same way,

text.font-family: 'IBM Plex Sans', 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif

g.text: but it is not 'vertex order'. RemoveRedundantEdges() calls the virtual GetTopologicalOrdering, so on a ScheduleEventDag it also uses the job-priority order.
